title: No musicians in the family; ukulele contest and first banjo
summary: His family had no musicians; he won a ukulele contest, got a banjo with LaRocca help, and took lessons from Boyto.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: What about anybody in your family? Did they help you? Did you have any musicians in your family at all?

No, my mother told me when I was smaller. I had uncle played, but my mother bought a piano years back for my brother and sister, and we lived on 4530 South Rousin Street, but they never did learn anything on the piano. And I never did learn, but I was determined to learn how to learn. About stuff

play. And I came back from Chicago and after I come back from Chicago, well I was visiting some of my friends at 2622 Gender Street where I once attended private school, grade school, and Miss Albert Annis was one of the teacher's sisters, said you helped my brother Fred to cut this grass, I'll teach you how to play the ukulele. So I loved the tones of the ukulele, when you know uk was out. And well Morris Music Store was on Ramport Street then and they had a contest with ukulele. Well I won the contest and to learn how to play piano or banjo or something like that. But I never did have a chance because he couldn't keep sufficient teachers. He'd get a lot of teachers there but they could play but they couldn't read. And my determination was to learn how to read. And I was masked on the corner of the day and I happened to be on Perrette between Cadys and the 4600 block. La Rocka's, they got a place back on Carlton Avenue, they call it Uncle Jim's. Well they had some of their relatives, once was the first one that put jazz on records, La Rocka's, you know Dixieland, band. And they heard me play the ukulele, you know like on Carnival Day we had kazooks and everything. We had a band. We just hummed around there and my doctor heard me play. So they got a pool and they got a pool up and they gave me some money to make a deposit on a banjo at G.C. Coyne, which was on Corontale Street, where Mr. Philip Boyto was there. And he didn't teach color at that time but I used to, after my teacher went back on the boat, he went back for working for Strepler, but Dewey Jackson had one of the boats in charge in St. Louis so he went back up there. And Mr. Boyto seen that I was anxious and after he used to teach me at my house, you know what I'm saying, so I used to go there and take lessons from him. And then from then on I got it and them, they got me a job of running on a boat playing music, and from then I just started and picked up what I could.
You didn't know your uncle's name that played music on there, that your mother played
